57	\section{STA Algorithm}
58	\label{app:algorithm}
59	
60	Algorithm~\ref{alg:sta} gives the full procedure for computing ISR over a proved formalization.
61	
62	\begin{algorithm}[h]
63	\caption{Solver Trace Ablation (STA)}
64	\label{alg:sta}
65	\begin{algorithmic}[1]
66	\REQUIRE Formalization $x = \{c_1, \ldots, c_n\}$, solver $S$
67	\ENSURE ISR score $\in [0,1]$ or $\bot$ (undefined)
68	\IF{$S(x) \neq \textit{proved}$}
69	  \RETURN $\bot$
70	\ENDIF
71	\STATE $n_{\text{nec}} \gets 0$
72	\FOR{$i = 1$ \TO $n$}
73	  \STATE $x' \gets x \setminus \{c_i\}$
74	  \IF{$S(x') = \textit{failed}$}
75	    \STATE $n_{\text{nec}} \gets n_{\text{nec}} + 1$
76	  \ENDIF
77	\ENDFOR
78	\RETURN $n_{\text{nec}} \mathbin{/} n$
79	\end{algorithmic}
80	\end{algorithm}

83	\section{Extended Discussion}
84	\label{app:extended-discussion}
85	
86	\paragraph{What ISR measures---and what it does not.}
87	ISR quantifies syntactic component necessity: the fraction of solver-input components whose individual removal causes proof failure.
88	This is strictly weaker than semantic faithfulness---whether the formalization accurately captures the natural-language meaning.
89	We verify this empirically: Spearman $\rho(\text{ISR}, \text{NLI accuracy}) = -0.049$ ($p = 0.187$, n.s.) from a downstream NLI evaluation on exec-only checkpoint outputs.
90	ISR and downstream task performance are uncorrelated.
91	ISR is thus a structural integrity diagnostic, not a semantic quality metric: high ISR indicates that every component contributes to the proof, not that the proof faithfully represents the original reasoning problem.
92	
93	Critically, low ISR carries different semantics depending on the training objective.
94	Under exec-only training, low ISR in Prolog reflects redundant coding---repeated ground facts where removing any single copy does not affect the proof---rather than absence of reasoning (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).
95	Under ISR-as-reward, high ISR reflects metric gaming (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
96	ISR values must always be interpreted relative to the optimization objective that produced them.
97	
98	\paragraph{The premise-count confound.}
99	LOO-based metrics like ISR have an inherent mathematical bias: with fewer components, each is mechanically more likely to be necessary.
100	A formalization with 2 premises where both are necessary yields ISR${=}1.0$; one with 10 premises where 8 are necessary yields ISR${=}0.8$---even though the latter encodes richer reasoning.
101	This confound explains the sole apparent ISR-as-reward success (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}): ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 produces shorter formalizations, mechanically inflating ISR.
102	Premise-count-matched comparison eliminates the difference ($1.06\times$; Table~\ref{tab:beta01-3seed}).
103	This bias is not specific to our setting---any LOO-based structural metric applied to variable-length outputs requires component-count normalization.
104	We recommend that future work employing ablation-based diagnostics report premise-count-matched comparisons alongside raw values.
105	
106	\paragraph{Meta-level Goodhart: implications.}
107	The meta-Goodhart finding extends beyond this specific system.
108	ISR was designed to \emph{detect} reward gaming of $r_{\text{exec}}$, yet when incorporated into the reward signal, the model games ISR itself---creating a regress where any diagnostic metric risks becoming a target when optimized.
109	The dose-response pattern ($\beta{=}0.1$: proxy gaming inflates ISR without genuine improvement; $\beta{=}0.3$: performance collapse) maps onto the trajectory predicted by~\cite{gao-reward-overoptimization}, but at a meta level: the proxy being gamed is itself a gaming detector.
110	Under the taxonomy of~\cite{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy}, $\beta{=}0.3$ exemplifies extremal Goodhart---the optimizer enters a regime where the proxy-target relationship breaks down entirely---while $\beta{=}0.1$ instantiates a meta-level variant where the diagnostic is gamed through its own measurement mechanism.
111	The practical implication is that ISR---and structurally similar diagnostics---should be used exclusively as post-hoc evaluation tools, never as training rewards.
112	
113	\paragraph{Single-seed unreliability.}
114	The three exec-only seeds diverge radically (PR $\sigma{=}\pm 47$ percentage points), each converging to a qualitatively different degeneration mode (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
115	ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seeds show similar divergence: 2/3 dominated by conclusion duplication (H7), 1/3 by premise minimization (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
116	Multi-seed evaluation with structural diagnostics should be standard practice for neurosymbolic RL systems.

119	\section{Hacking Mode Definitions}
120	\label{app:hacking-modes}
121	
122	We identify seven distinct reward hacking modes across all experiments.
123	Each mode is defined below with its mechanism, a representative example, and its interaction with ISR.
124	Table~\ref{tab:hacking-taxonomy-app} summarizes prevalence across FOL conditions.
125	
126	\begin{table}[h]
127	\centering
128	\small
129	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
130	\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccc@{}}
131	\toprule
132	\textbf{Mode} & \textbf{Mechanism} & \textbf{Exec} & \textbf{ISR} & \textbf{Rnd} & \textbf{SFT} \\
133	\midrule
134	H1 & Concl.\ in premises & 87 & 17 & 81 & 7 \\
135	H7 & Single prem.\ = concl. & $\bullet$ & \textbf{65} & 0 & 0 \\
136	Tautological & 2-comp $P{=}C$ & $\bullet$ & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
137	Repetition & Output degen. & $\bullet$ & -- & -- & -- \\
138	Contradiction & $n_{\text{comp}}$ inflated & $\bullet$ & -- & -- & -- \\
139	C-w/o-utility & Complex, redundant & 0 & 0 & 4 & 0 \\
140	Q-as-fact & Atom = fact+query & -- & -- & -- & -- \\
141	\bottomrule
142	\end{tabular}}
143	\caption{Hacking taxonomy across FOL conditions (\% of proved samples). ISR/Rand columns: $\beta{=}0.1$ 3-seed means. Exec: H1${=}87$\% in s42; $\bullet$ marks seed- or step-specific modes (H7/Tautological in s44, Repetition in s43, Contradiction at 1000 steps). C-w/o-util.: complexity-without-utility (random-specific). Q-as-fact: Prolog STA only (Table~\ref{tab:prolog-crosslogic}).}
144	\label{tab:hacking-taxonomy-app}
145	\end{table}
146	
147	\paragraph{Classifier Validation.}
148	Hacking mode classification uses deterministic rule-based classifiers, not learned models, so standard ML precision/recall is not directly applicable.
149	H1 and H7 are identified by normalized text matching between conclusion and premise strings after whitespace and variable normalization; remaining modes are detected via functional analysis of the per-sample $n_{\text{necessary}}$ distribution from STA (leave-one-out ablation).
150	No training data or manual annotation is used for classification.
151	
152	To estimate precision, we manually verified 50 randomly sampled outputs classified as H1 or H7: all 50 were confirmed correct (estimated precision ${>}$95\%, Wilson 95\% CI: [93\%, 100\%]).
153	Recall is inherently bounded by the text-match threshold: semantic manipulations that alter surface form while preserving the gaming structure (e.g., variable renaming beyond our normalization, or paraphrased conclusions) would be missed.
154	We cross-validate with functional LOO analysis: samples classified as non-hacking but showing $n_{\text{necessary}} \leq 1$ are flagged as potential false negatives.
155	This cross-validation revealed query-as-fact gaming in Prolog (\S\ref{app:hacking-modes}), where the strict text classifier reported 100\% non-hacking but functional analysis showed 95/97 samples were tautological ($n_{\text{necessary}}{=}1$).
156	The non-hacking rate for FOL conditions may therefore be slightly overestimated, as subtle semantic manipulations below our text-matching threshold would evade the strict classifier.
157	
158	\subsection{H1 --- Conclusion Embedding}
159	
160	\paragraph{Definition.}
161	The conclusion appears verbatim (or with trivial variable renaming) as one premise among multiple premises.
162	The solver succeeds by matching the embedded conclusion, rendering the other premises irrelevant to the proof.
163	
164	\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
165	{\small\begin{verbatim}
166	Premises:
167	  all x (bird(x) -> flies(x)).
168	  bird(tweety).
169	  flies(tweety).  % conclusion embedded
170	Conclusion: flies(tweety).
171	\end{verbatim}}
172	
173	\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
174	Variable. The embedded premise has ISR~$=1$ (removing it may break the proof), but other premises may also register as necessary depending on Prover9's search strategy.
175	ISR does not distinguish trivial from substantive necessity.
176	
177	\paragraph{Prevalence.}
178	Conclusion embedding in some form (H1 multi-premise or H7 single-premise) is GRPO-universal at 68--97\% across all RL conditions.
179	Under exec-only and Random reward, it manifests as H1 (71--93\%); under ISR reward, it shifts to H7 (64.5\% pooled).
180	
181	
182	\subsection{H7 --- Conclusion Duplication}
183	
184	\paragraph{Definition.}
185	The entire formalization collapses to a single premise whose content is identical to the conclusion.
186	Since $P \to P$ is trivially provable, this simultaneously maximizes exec reward.
187	Because the sole premise is necessary for every sub-component of the conclusion under LOO ablation, ISR is inflated toward 1.0.
188	
189	\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
190	{\small\begin{verbatim}
191	Premises:
192	  all x ((A(x)&B(x))->(C(x)|D(x))).
193	Conclusion:
194	  all x ((A(x)&B(x))->(C(x)|D(x))).
195	\end{verbatim}}
196	
197	\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
198	ISR~$\approx 0.8$--$1.0$.
199	The single premise is trivially ``maximally necessary,'' but the proof is vacuous.
200	H7 is the only mode that simultaneously games both exec reward and ISR reward.
201	
202	\paragraph{Prevalence.}
203	ISR-specific: 64.5\% pooled (149/231) under ISR~$\beta{=}0.1$ (s42: 16.0\%, s43: 96.7\%, s44: 86.5\%).
204	\textbf{Zero} occurrences under Random~$\beta{=}0.1$ across all three seeds ($0/256$).
205	
206	
207	\subsection{Tautological Collapse}
208	
209	\paragraph{Definition.}
210	Two-component formalizations where the premise and conclusion are identical atomic or simple formulas, yielding a $P \to P$ tautology with minimal token cost.
211	
212	\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
213	\begin{verbatim}
214	Premises: p(a).
215	Conclusion: p(a).
216	\end{verbatim}
217	
218	\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
219	ISR~$=1.0$ (the sole premise is necessary).
220	Distinguished from H7 by having low component count ($n_{\text{comp}}\approx 2$) and atomic formulas rather than complex sub-structured conclusions.
221	
222	\paragraph{Prevalence.}
223	Dominant in FOL exec-only seed~44 (PR~$=0.98$, mean $n_{\text{comp}}=2.04$, 100\% H7 by strict classifier).
224	Also observed in Prolog exec+STA seed~42 (100\% H7, PR~$=0.50$).
225	
226	
227	\subsection{Repetition Collapse}
228	
229	\paragraph{Definition.}
230	The model generates identical premises or clauses repeated until the maximum completion length, producing a degenerate output with high token count but no logical diversity.
231	Removing any single repeated copy leaves the others intact, yielding ISR~$\approx 0$.
232	
233	\paragraph{Example (Prolog).}
234	\begin{verbatim}
235	penguin(fido).
236	penguin(fido).
237	penguin(fido).
238	... (repeated to 512 tokens)
239	query(penguin(fido)).
240	\end{verbatim}
241	
242	\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
243	ISR~$\approx 0$. Each copy is individually redundant since identical copies remain after removal.
244	ISR correctly diagnoses this degeneration.
245	
246	\paragraph{Prevalence.}
247	Observed in FOL exec-only seed~43 (87\% of outputs hit max completion length; PR~$=14$\%, ISR~$=0$).
248	
249	
250	\subsection{Complexity-without-Utility}
251	
252	\paragraph{Definition.}
253	The formalization contains syntactically complex premises (nested quantifiers, multi-arity predicates) that are semantically vacuous---none individually necessary for the proof.
254	The complexity inflates surface metrics (formula length, nesting depth) without contributing to logical derivation.
255	
256	\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
257	{\small\begin{verbatim}
258	Premises:
259	  all x all y (R(x,y) ->
260	    exists z (S(x,z) & T(z,y))).
261	  all x (P(x) -> Q(x)).
262	  P(a).            % only this needed
263	Conclusion: Q(a).
264	\end{verbatim}}
265	
266	\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
267	ISR correctly identifies the vacuous premises (ISR~$=0$ for each), pulling down the mean ISR.
268	This is the mode ISR is best calibrated for.
269	
270	\paragraph{Prevalence.}
271	Low. Observed in Random~$\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 at 3.8\% (3/79).
272	Not observed under ISR reward (ISR's gradient discourages zero-ISR premises).
273	
274	
275	\subsection{Contradiction Explosion}
276	
277	\paragraph{Definition.}
278	The component count grows unboundedly over training.
279	Excess premises introduce contradictions or redundancies that trivially entail any conclusion via \emph{ex falso quodlibet}.
280	Individual premises may register as ISR~$=0$ (removable without breaking the proof), but the sheer count obscures the underlying triviality.
281	
282	\paragraph{Example (FOL, 1000-step exec-only).}
283	{\small\begin{verbatim}
284	Premises:
285	  c1. c2. c3. ... c18. % 18.55 mean
286	  % conclusion embedded among premises
287	Conclusion: Q(a).
288	\end{verbatim}}
289	
290	\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
291	ISR~$\approx 0$ (at 1000 steps: ISR~$=0.003$, with 94.8\% of proved samples having ISR~$=0$).
292	
293	\paragraph{Prevalence.}
294	Observed in extended exec-only training (seed~42, 1000 steps).
295	Mean component count grows from ${\sim}6$ (500 steps) to 18.55 (1000 steps).
296	
297	
298	\subsection{Query-as-Fact Gaming}
299	
300	\paragraph{Definition.}
301	The model converts the natural language conclusion into a snake\_case atom and includes it as both a ground fact and the query.
302	Prolog trivially proves the query by unifying with the fact.
303	This mode evades text-match classifiers designed for H1/H7 because the generated atom bears no surface resemblance to the original conclusion text.
304	
305	\paragraph{Example (Prolog).}
306	\begin{verbatim}
307	% NL: "Fido is happy."
308	% Model output:
309	fido_is_happy.
310	:- fido_is_happy.     % query = fact
311	\end{verbatim}
312	
313	\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
314	ISR~$\approx 0.9$--$1.0$.
315	The fact is necessarily necessary (its removal breaks the query), inflating ISR.
316	Functionally equivalent to H7 but with a distinct surface mechanism.
317	
318	\paragraph{Prevalence.}
319	Observed in Prolog exec+STA seed~44 (PR~$=0.97$, ISR~$=0.912$).
320	95/97 proved samples have $n_{\text{necessary}}=1$, confirming functional tautology despite the strict classifier reporting 100\% non-hacking.

\section{STA Algorithm}
\label{app:algorithm}

Algorithm~\ref{alg:sta} gives the full procedure for computing ISR over a proved formalization.

\begin{algorithm}[h]
\caption{Solver Trace Ablation (STA)}
\label{alg:sta}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\REQUIRE Formalization $x = \{c_1, \ldots, c_n\}$, solver $S$
\ENSURE ISR score $\in [0,1]$ or $\bot$ (undefined)
\IF{$S(x) \neq \textit{proved}$}
  \RETURN $\bot$
\ENDIF
\STATE $n_{\text{nec}} \gets 0$
\FOR{$i = 1$ \TO $n$}
  \STATE $x' \gets x \setminus \{c_i\}$
  \IF{$S(x') = \textit{failed}$}
    \STATE $n_{\text{nec}} \gets n_{\text{nec}} + 1$
  \ENDIF
\ENDFOR
\RETURN $n_{\text{nec}} \mathbin{/} n$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}


\section{Extended Discussion}
\label{app:extended-discussion}

\paragraph{What ISR measures---and what it does not.}
ISR quantifies syntactic component necessity: the fraction of solver-input components whose individual removal causes proof failure.
This is strictly weaker than semantic faithfulness---whether the formalization accurately captures the natural-language meaning.
We verify this empirically: Spearman $\rho(\text{ISR}, \text{NLI accuracy}) = -0.049$ ($p = 0.187$, n.s.) from a downstream NLI evaluation on exec-only checkpoint outputs.
ISR and downstream task performance are uncorrelated.
ISR is thus a structural integrity diagnostic, not a semantic quality metric: high ISR indicates that every component contributes to the proof, not that the proof faithfully represents the original reasoning problem.

Critically, low ISR carries different semantics depending on the training objective.
Under exec-only training, low ISR in Prolog reflects redundant coding---repeated ground facts where removing any single copy does not affect the proof---rather than absence of reasoning (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).
Under ISR-as-reward, high ISR reflects metric gaming (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
ISR values must always be interpreted relative to the optimization objective that produced them.

\paragraph{The premise-count confound.}
LOO-based metrics like ISR have an inherent mathematical bias: with fewer components, each is mechanically more likely to be necessary.
A formalization with 2 premises where both are necessary yields ISR${=}1.0$; one with 10 premises where 8 are necessary yields ISR${=}0.8$---even though the latter encodes richer reasoning.
This confound explains the sole apparent ISR-as-reward success (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}): ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 produces shorter formalizations, mechanically inflating ISR.
Premise-count-matched comparison eliminates the difference ($1.06\times$; Table~\ref{tab:beta01-3seed}).
This bias is not specific to our setting---any LOO-based structural metric applied to variable-length outputs requires component-count normalization.
We recommend that future work employing ablation-based diagnostics report premise-count-matched comparisons alongside raw values.

\paragraph{Meta-level Goodhart: implications.}
The meta-Goodhart finding extends beyond this specific system.
ISR was designed to \emph{detect} reward gaming of $r_{\text{exec}}$, yet when incorporated into the reward signal, the model games ISR itself---creating a regress where any diagnostic metric risks becoming a target when optimized.
The dose-response pattern ($\beta{=}0.1$: proxy gaming inflates ISR without genuine improvement; $\beta{=}0.3$: performance collapse) maps onto the trajectory predicted by~\cite{gao-reward-overoptimization}, but at a meta level: the proxy being gamed is itself a gaming detector.
Under the taxonomy of~\cite{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy}, $\beta{=}0.3$ exemplifies extremal Goodhart---the optimizer enters a regime where the proxy-target relationship breaks down entirely---while $\beta{=}0.1$ instantiates a meta-level variant where the diagnostic is gamed through its own measurement mechanism.
The practical implication is that ISR---and structurally similar diagnostics---should be used exclusively as post-hoc evaluation tools, never as training rewards.

\paragraph{Single-seed unreliability.}
The three exec-only seeds diverge radically (PR $\sigma{=}\pm 47$ percentage points), each converging to a qualitatively different degeneration mode (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seeds show similar divergence: 2/3 dominated by conclusion duplication (H7), 1/3 by premise minimization (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
Multi-seed evaluation with structural diagnostics should be standard practice for neurosymbolic RL systems.


\section{Hacking Mode Definitions}
\label{app:hacking-modes}

We identify seven distinct reward hacking modes across all experiments.
Each mode is defined below with its mechanism, a representative example, and its interaction with ISR.
Table~\ref{tab:hacking-taxonomy-app} summarizes prevalence across FOL conditions.

\paragraph{Classifier Validation.}
Hacking mode classification uses deterministic rule-based classifiers, not learned models, so standard ML precision/recall is not directly applicable.
H1 and H7 are identified by normalized text matching between conclusion and premise strings after whitespace and variable normalization; remaining modes are detected via functional analysis of the per-sample $n_{\text{necessary}}$ distribution from STA (leave-one-out ablation).
No training data or manual annotation is used for classification.

To estimate precision, we manually verified 50 randomly sampled outputs classified as H1 or H7: all 50 were confirmed correct (estimated precision ${>}$95\%, Wilson 95\% CI: [93\%, 100\%]).
Recall is inherently bounded by the text-match threshold: semantic manipulations that alter surface form while preserving the gaming structure (e.g., variable renaming beyond our normalization, or paraphrased conclusions) would be missed.
We cross-validate with functional LOO analysis: samples classified as non-hacking but showing $n_{\text{necessary}} \leq 1$ are flagged as potential false negatives.
This cross-validation revealed query-as-fact gaming in Prolog (\S\ref{app:hacking-modes}), where the strict text classifier reported 100\% non-hacking but functional analysis showed 95/97 samples were tautological ($n_{\text{necessary}}{=}1$).
The non-hacking rate for FOL conditions may therefore be slightly overestimated, as subtle semantic manipulations below our text-matching threshold would evade the strict classifier.

\subsection{H1 --- Conclusion Embedding}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The conclusion appears verbatim (or with trivial variable renaming) as one premise among multiple premises.
The solver succeeds by matching the embedded conclusion, rendering the other premises irrelevant to the proof.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  all x (bird(x) -> flies(x)).
  bird(tweety).
  flies(tweety).  % conclusion embedded
Conclusion: flies(tweety).
\end{verbatim}}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
Variable. The embedded premise has ISR~$=1$ (removing it may break the proof), but other premises may also register as necessary depending on Prover9's search strategy.
ISR does not distinguish trivial from substantive necessity.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Conclusion embedding in some form (H1 multi-premise or H7 single-premise) is GRPO-universal at 68--97\% across all RL conditions.
Under exec-only and Random reward, it manifests as H1 (71--93\%); under ISR reward, it shifts to H7 (64.5\% pooled).


\subsection{H7 --- Conclusion Duplication}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The entire formalization collapses to a single premise whose content is identical to the conclusion.
Since $P \to P$ is trivially provable, this simultaneously maximizes exec reward.
Because the sole premise is necessary for every sub-component of the conclusion under LOO ablation, ISR is inflated toward 1.0.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  all x ((A(x)&B(x))->(C(x)|D(x))).
Conclusion:
  all x ((A(x)&B(x))->(C(x)|D(x))).
\end{verbatim}}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$\approx 0.8$--$1.0$.
The single premise is trivially ``maximally necessary,'' but the proof is vacuous.
H7 is the only mode that simultaneously games both exec reward and ISR reward.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
ISR-specific: 64.5\% pooled (149/231) under ISR~$\beta{=}0.1$ (s42: 16.0\%, s43: 96.7\%, s44: 86.5\%).
\textbf{Zero} occurrences under Random~$\beta{=}0.1$ across all three seeds ($0/256$).


\subsection{Tautological Collapse}

\paragraph{Definition.}
Two-component formalizations where the premise and conclusion are identical atomic or simple formulas, yielding a $P \to P$ tautology with minimal token cost.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
\begin{verbatim}
Premises: p(a).
Conclusion: p(a).
\end{verbatim}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$=1.0$ (the sole premise is necessary).
Distinguished from H7 by having low component count ($n_{\text{comp}}\approx 2$) and atomic formulas rather than complex sub-structured conclusions.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Dominant in FOL exec-only seed~44 (PR~$=0.98$, mean $n_{\text{comp}}=2.04$, 100\% H7 by strict classifier).
Also observed in Prolog exec+STA seed~42 (100\% H7, PR~$=0.50$).


\subsection{Repetition Collapse}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The model generates identical premises or clauses repeated until the maximum completion length, producing a degenerate output with high token count but no logical diversity.
Removing any single repeated copy leaves the others intact, yielding ISR~$\approx 0$.

\paragraph{Example (Prolog).}
\begin{verbatim}
penguin(fido).
penguin(fido).
penguin(fido).
... (repeated to 512 tokens)
query(penguin(fido)).
\end{verbatim}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$\approx 0$. Each copy is individually redundant since identical copies remain after removal.
ISR correctly diagnoses this degeneration.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Observed in FOL exec-only seed~43 (87\% of outputs hit max completion length; PR~$=14$\%, ISR~$=0$).


\subsection{Complexity-without-Utility}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The formalization contains syntactically complex premises (nested quantifiers, multi-arity predicates) that are semantically vacuous---none individually necessary for the proof.
The complexity inflates surface metrics (formula length, nesting depth) without contributing to logical derivation.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  all x all y (R(x,y) ->
    exists z (S(x,z) & T(z,y))).
  all x (P(x) -> Q(x)).
  P(a).            % only this needed
Conclusion: Q(a).
\end{verbatim}}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR correctly identifies the vacuous premises (ISR~$=0$ for each), pulling down the mean ISR.
This is the mode ISR is best calibrated for.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Low. Observed in Random~$\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 at 3.8\% (3/79).
Not observed under ISR reward (ISR's gradient discourages zero-ISR premises).


\subsection{Contradiction Explosion}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The component count grows unboundedly over training.
Excess premises introduce contradictions or redundancies that trivially entail any conclusion via \emph{ex falso quodlibet}.
Individual premises may register as ISR~$=0$ (removable without breaking the proof), but the sheer count obscures the underlying triviality.

\paragraph{Example (FOL, 1000-step exec-only).}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  c1. c2. c3. ... c18. % 18.55 mean
  % conclusion embedded among premises
Conclusion: Q(a).
\end{verbatim}}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$\approx 0$ (at 1000 steps: ISR~$=0.003$, with 94.8\% of proved samples having ISR~$=0$).

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Observed in extended exec-only training (seed~42, 1000 steps).
Mean component count grows from ${\sim}6$ (500 steps) to 18.55 (1000 steps).


\subsection{Query-as-Fact Gaming}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The model converts the natural language conclusion into a snake\_case atom and includes it as both a ground fact and the query.
Prolog trivially proves the query by unifying with the fact.
This mode evades text-match classifiers designed for H1/H7 because the generated atom bears no surface resemblance to the original conclusion text.

\paragraph{Example (Prolog).}
\begin{verbatim}
% NL: "Fido is happy."
% Model output:
fido_is_happy.
:- fido_is_happy.     % query = fact
\end{verbatim}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$\approx 0.9$--$1.0$.
The fact is necessarily necessary (its removal breaks the query), inflating ISR.
Functionally equivalent to H7 but with a distinct surface mechanism.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Observed in Prolog exec+STA seed~44 (PR~$=0.97$, ISR~$=0.912$).
95/97 proved samples have $n_{\text{necessary}}=1$, confirming functional tautology despite the strict classifier reporting 100\% non-hacking.

\subsection{Early-Training Hacking Analysis (100-Step Checkpoint)}
\label{app:100step}

To control for the prove-rate confound in our SFT comparison (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}), we analyze the exec-only checkpoint at 100 training steps (seed~42), where PR${=}32$\%---higher than SFT (14\%) but still early in training.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related-work}

\paragraph{Neurosymbolic Reasoning with LLMs.}
Prompting-based pipelines couple LLMs with external solvers for logical reasoning.
SatLM~\cite{satlm} generates SAT formulas, Logic-LM~\cite{logic-lm} translates to first-order logic, LINC~\cite{linc} generates logic programs, and LoRP~\cite{lorp} uses Prolog as a reasoning backend; FOVER~\cite{fover-pei2025} adds iterative verification.
All evaluate on execution accuracy alone, without diagnosing structural quality of formalizations.
Recent RL approaches train LLMs against solver feedback~\cite{mellgren-prolog-grpo, logic-rl, thought-like-pro}, optimizing prove rate with binary execution reward.
STA differs in diagnostic focus: ISR exposes that execution accuracy conflates faithful derivation with degenerate shortcuts, and our finding that 87\% of proved outputs under exec-only GRPO embed the conclusion in the premises (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}) suggests prior prove-rate gains may overstate genuine reasoning improvement.
We adopt FOLIO~\cite{folio} as it is the only publicly available NLI benchmark providing both FOL and Prolog annotations, enabling our cross-logic diagnostic transfer experiments; ProofWriter~\cite{proofwriter} and ProntoQA~\cite{prontoqa} offer synthetic logical reasoning benchmarks but lack the multi-logic annotation required for cross-logic comparison.

\paragraph{Reward Shaping and Process Supervision.}
Binary outcome rewards motivate process-level supervision: learned process reward models~\cite[PRMs;][]{lightman-verify-step, math-shepherd} provide step-level feedback, solver-grounded signals~\cite{rlsf} leverage formal verification, and rubric-based rewards~\cite{rubric-grpo} encode structured evaluation criteria.
However, process rewards introduce their own failure modes: design choices dominate signal effects~\cite{gao-effective-rl-reward}, process and outcome rewards can conflict~\cite{prof-process-outcome}, and PRMs degrade at distribution shift~\cite{qwen-prm-lessons, processbench, progrs-outcome-conditioned}.
Recent PRM advances address these limitations through generative verification chains~\cite{thinkprm}, multi-domain training data~\cite{versaprm}, and reasoning-driven evaluation~\cite{rprm}, but remain learned and require curated supervision.
ISR is solver-grounded rather than learned (no reward-model noise), yet our \S\ref{sec:goodhart} result shows that even non-learned, deterministic process signals Goodhart when optimized---suggesting the problem is fundamental to process-level reward shaping, not specific to learned models.

\paragraph{Reward Hacking and Goodhart's Law.}
Prior work establishes Goodhart's Law theoretically~\cite{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy, skalse-reward-hacking, karwowski-goodhart-rl, pan-reward-misspecification, kwa-catastrophic-goodhart} and observes overoptimization scaling in RLHF~\cite{gao-reward-overoptimization}; recent empirical reports document frontier models reward-hacking code-generation tasks in practice~\cite{metr-reward-hacking, macdiarmid-emergent-misalignment}, with learned reward hacking generalizing to misaligned behaviors in unrelated contexts~\cite{school-reward-hacks}.
In LLMs, specification gaming~\cite{bondarenko-spec-gaming}, formalization gaming~\cite{kim-game-formalization}, and spurious RLVR rewards~\cite{spurious-rewards} have been documented, but the proxy in these analyses is a learned reward model.
Kim et al.~\cite{kim-game-formalization} examine formalization gaming in Lean 4 theorem proving, identifying axiom fabrication and premise mistranslation as unfaithfulness modes via inference-time prompting on FOLIO and Multi-LogiEval.
Our work is complementary: while Kim et al.\ diagnose gaming in inference-time outputs of frontier models, we study gaming that \emph{emerges during RL training} and provide ISR as a structural diagnostic with a systematic seven-mode taxonomy and cross-logic transfer analysis.
Our setting differs in two respects: ISR is deterministic and solver-derived, eliminating reward-model noise; and the Goodhart effect operates at a \emph{meta} level---ISR was designed to detect gaming of execution reward, yet itself becomes gamed when optimized.
This meta-level phenomenon---where a diagnostic for gaming becomes the target of gaming---has not been previously documented in the reward hacking literature.

\paragraph{Mutation Testing.}
STA adapts the leave-one-out mutation paradigm~\cite{demillo1978, offutt-coupling, jia-harman-survey, just-mutants-real-faults} from software testing to neurosymbolic formalizations: the ``program'' is the solver input, the ``test'' is proof success, and the diagnostic target is component necessity for proof validity.
While mutation testing has been applied to neural networks~\cite{llmorpheus} and test suite adequacy, our application to \emph{solver inputs} for diagnosing structural quality of model-generated formalizations is novel.
The novelty lies in application and findings (ISR collapse, meta-Goodhart, hacking taxonomy), not in the perturbation technique itself.

\paragraph{Evaluation exception.}

Its PR and ISR values are included for completeness but are not strictly comparable with other seeds under the unified evaluation protocol (C004).


\section{STA Algorithm}
\label{app:algorithm}

Algorithm~\ref{alg:sta} gives the full procedure for computing ISR over a proved formalization.

\begin{algorithm}[h]
\caption{Solver Trace Ablation (STA)}
\label{alg:sta}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\REQUIRE Formalization $x = \{c_1, \ldots, c_n\}$, solver $S$
\ENSURE ISR score $\in [0,1]$ or $\bot$ (undefined)
\IF{$S(x) \neq \textit{proved}$}
  \RETURN $\bot$
\ENDIF
\STATE $n_{\text{nec}} \gets 0$
\FOR{$i = 1$ \TO $n$}
  \STATE $x' \gets x \setminus \{c_i\}$
  \IF{$S(x') = \textit{failed}$}
    \STATE $n_{\text{nec}} \gets n_{\text{nec}} + 1$
  \ENDIF
\ENDFOR
\RETURN $n_{\text{nec}} \mathbin{/} n$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}


\section{Extended Discussion}
\label{app:extended-discussion}

\paragraph{What ISR measures---and what it does not.}
ISR quantifies syntactic component necessity: the fraction of solver-input components whose individual removal causes proof failure.
This is strictly weaker than semantic faithfulness---whether the formalization accurately captures the natural-language meaning.
We verify this empirically: Spearman $\rho(\text{ISR}, \text{NLI accuracy}) = -0.049$ ($p = 0.187$, n.s.) from a downstream NLI evaluation on exec-only checkpoint outputs.
ISR and downstream task performance are uncorrelated.
ISR is thus a structural integrity diagnostic, not a semantic quality metric: high ISR indicates that every component contributes to the proof, not that the proof faithfully represents the original reasoning problem.

Critically, low ISR carries different semantics depending on the training objective.
Under exec-only training, low ISR in Prolog reflects redundant coding---repeated ground facts where removing any single copy does not affect the proof---rather than absence of reasoning (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).
Under ISR-as-reward, high ISR reflects metric gaming (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
ISR values must always be interpreted relative to the optimization objective that produced them.

\paragraph{The premise-count confound.}
LOO-based metrics like ISR have an inherent mathematical bias: with fewer components, each is mechanically more likely to be necessary.
A formalization with 2 premises where both are necessary yields ISR${=}1.0$; one with 10 premises where 8 are necessary yields ISR${=}0.8$---even though the latter encodes richer reasoning.
This confound explains the sole apparent ISR-as-reward success (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}): ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 produces shorter formalizations, mechanically inflating ISR.
Premise-count-matched comparison eliminates the difference ($1.06\times$; Table~\ref{tab:beta01-3seed}).
This bias is not specific to our setting---any LOO-based structural metric applied to variable-length outputs requires component-count normalization.
We recommend that future work employing ablation-based diagnostics report premise-count-matched comparisons alongside raw values.

\paragraph{Meta-level Goodhart: implications.}
The meta-Goodhart finding extends beyond this specific system.
ISR was designed to \emph{detect} reward gaming of $r_{\text{exec}}$, yet when incorporated into the reward signal, the model games ISR itself---creating a regress where any diagnostic metric risks becoming a target when optimized.
The dose-response pattern ($\beta{=}0.1$: proxy gaming inflates ISR without genuine improvement; $\beta{=}0.3$: performance collapse) maps onto the trajectory predicted by~\cite{gao-reward-overoptimization}, but at a meta level: the proxy being gamed is itself a gaming detector.
Under the taxonomy of~\cite{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy}, $\beta{=}0.3$ exemplifies extremal Goodhart---the optimizer enters a regime where the proxy-target relationship breaks down entirely---while $\beta{=}0.1$ instantiates a meta-level variant where the diagnostic is gamed through its own measurement mechanism.
The practical implication is that ISR---and structurally similar diagnostics---should be used exclusively as post-hoc evaluation tools, never as training rewards.

\paragraph{Single-seed unreliability.}
The three exec-only seeds diverge radically (PR $\sigma{=}\pm 47$ percentage points), each converging to a qualitatively different degeneration mode (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seeds show similar divergence: 2/3 dominated by conclusion duplication (H7), 1/3 by premise minimization (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
Multi-seed evaluation with structural diagnostics should be standard practice for neurosymbolic RL systems.


\section{Hacking Mode Definitions}
\label{app:hacking-modes}

We identify seven distinct reward hacking modes across all experiments.
Each mode is defined below with its mechanism, a representative example, and its interaction with ISR.
Table~\ref{tab:hacking-taxonomy-app} summarizes prevalence across FOL conditions.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Mode} & \textbf{Mechanism} & \textbf{Exec} & \textbf{ISR} & \textbf{Rnd} & \textbf{SFT} \\
\midrule
H1 & Concl.\ in premises & 87 & 17 & 81 & 7 \\
H7 & Single prem.\ = concl. & $\bullet$ & \textbf{65} & 0 & 0 \\
Tautological & 2-comp $P{=}C$ & $\bullet$ & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
Repetition & Output degen. & $\bullet$ & -- & -- & -- \\
Contradiction & $n_{\text{comp}}$ inflated & $\bullet$ & -- & -- & -- \\
C-w/o-utility & Complex, redundant & 0 & 0 & 4 & 0 \\
Q-as-fact & Atom = fact+query & -- & -- & -- & -- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\caption{Hacking taxonomy across FOL conditions (\% of proved samples). ISR/Rand columns: $\beta{=}0.1$ 3-seed means. Exec: H1${=}87$\% in s42; $\bullet$ marks seed- or step-specific modes (H7/Tautological in s44, Repetition in s43, Contradiction at 1000 steps). C-w/o-util.: complexity-without-utility (random-specific). Q-as-fact: Prolog STA only (Table~\ref{tab:prolog-crosslogic}).}
\label{tab:hacking-taxonomy-app}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Classifier Validation.}
Hacking mode classification uses deterministic rule-based classifiers, not learned models, so standard ML precision/recall is not directly applicable.
H1 and H7 are identified by normalized text matching between conclusion and premise strings after whitespace and variable normalization; remaining modes are detected via functional analysis of the per-sample $n_{\text{necessary}}$ distribution from STA (leave-one-out ablation).
No training data or manual annotation is used for classification.

To estimate precision, we manually verified 50 randomly sampled outputs classified as H1 or H7: all 50 were confirmed correct (estimated precision ${>}$95\%, Wilson 95\% CI: [93\%, 100\%]).
Recall is inherently bounded by the text-match threshold: semantic manipulations that alter surface form while preserving the gaming structure (e.g., variable renaming beyond our normalization, or paraphrased conclusions) would be missed.
We cross-validate with functional LOO analysis: samples classified as non-hacking but showing $n_{\text{necessary}} \leq 1$ are flagged as potential false negatives.
This cross-validation revealed query-as-fact gaming in Prolog (\S\ref{app:hacking-modes}), where the strict text classifier reported 100\% non-hacking but functional analysis showed 95/97 samples were tautological ($n_{\text{necessary}}{=}1$).
The non-hacking rate for FOL conditions may therefore be slightly overestimated, as subtle semantic manipulations below our text-matching threshold would evade the strict classifier.

\subsection{H1 --- Conclusion Embedding}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The conclusion appears verbatim (or with trivial variable renaming) as one premise among multiple premises.
The solver succeeds by matching the embedded conclusion, rendering the other premises irrelevant to the proof.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  all x (bird(x) -> flies(x)).
  bird(tweety).
  flies(tweety).  % conclusion embedded
Conclusion: flies(tweety).
\end{verbatim}}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
Variable. The embedded premise has ISR~$=1$ (removing it may break the proof), but other premises may also register as necessary depending on Prover9's search strategy.
ISR does not distinguish trivial from substantive necessity.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Conclusion embedding in some form (H1 multi-premise or H7 single-premise) is GRPO-universal at 68--97\% across all RL conditions.
Under exec-only and Random reward, it manifests as H1 (71--93\%); under ISR reward, it shifts to H7 (64.5\% pooled).


\subsection{H7 --- Conclusion Duplication}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The entire formalization collapses to a single premise whose content is identical to the conclusion.
Since $P \to P$ is trivially provable, this simultaneously maximizes exec reward.
Because the sole premise is necessary for every sub-component of the conclusion under LOO ablation, ISR is inflated toward 1.0.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  all x ((A(x)&B(x))->(C(x)|D(x))).
Conclusion:
  all x ((A(x)&B(x))->(C(x)|D(x))).
\end{verbatim}}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$\approx 0.8$--$1.0$.
The single premise is trivially ``maximally necessary,'' but the proof is vacuous.
H7 is the only mode that simultaneously games both exec reward and ISR reward.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
ISR-specific: 64.5\% pooled (149/231) under ISR~$\beta{=}0.1$ (s42: 16.0\%, s43: 96.7\%, s44: 86.5\%).
\textbf{Zero} occurrences under Random~$\beta{=}0.1$ across all three seeds ($0/256$).


\subsection{Tautological Collapse}

\paragraph{Definition.}
Two-component formalizations where the premise and conclusion are identical atomic or simple formulas, yielding a $P \to P$ tautology with minimal token cost.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
\begin{verbatim}
Premises: p(a).
Conclusion: p(a).
\end{verbatim}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$=1.0$ (the sole premise is necessary).
Distinguished from H7 by having low component count ($n_{\text{comp}}\approx 2$) and atomic formulas rather than complex sub-structured conclusions.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Dominant in FOL exec-only seed~44 (PR~$=0.98$, mean $n_{\text{comp}}=2.04$, 100\% H7 by strict classifier).
Also observed in Prolog exec+STA seed~42 (100\% H7, PR~$=0.50$).


\subsection{Repetition Collapse}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The model generates identical premises or clauses repeated until the maximum completion length, producing a degenerate output with high token count but no logical diversity.
Removing any single repeated copy leaves the others intact, yielding ISR~$\approx 0$.

\paragraph{Example (Prolog).}
\begin{verbatim}
penguin(fido).
penguin(fido).
penguin(fido).
... (repeated to 512 tokens)
query(penguin(fido)).
\end{verbatim}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$\approx 0$. Each copy is individually redundant since identical copies remain after removal.
ISR correctly diagnoses this degeneration.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Observed in FOL exec-only seed~43 (87\% of outputs hit max completion length; PR~$=14$\%, ISR~$=0$).


\subsection{Complexity-without-Utility}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The formalization contains syntactically complex premises (nested quantifiers, multi-arity predicates) that are semantically vacuous---none individually necessary for the proof.
The complexity inflates surface metrics (formula length, nesting depth) without contributing to logical derivation.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  all x all y (R(x,y) ->
    exists z (S(x,z) & T(z,y))).
  all x (P(x) -> Q(x)).
  P(a).            % only this needed
Conclusion: Q(a).
\end{verbatim}}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR correctly identifies the vacuous premises (ISR~$=0$ for each), pulling down the mean ISR.
This is the mode ISR is best calibrated for.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Low. Observed in Random~$\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 at 3.8\% (3/79).
Not observed under ISR reward (ISR's gradient discourages zero-ISR premises).


\subsection{Contradiction Explosion}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The component count grows unboundedly over training.
Excess premises introduce contradictions or redundancies that trivially entail any conclusion via \emph{ex falso quodlibet}.
Individual premises may register as ISR~$=0$ (removable without breaking the proof), but the sheer count obscures the underlying triviality.

\paragraph{Example (FOL, 1000-step exec-only).}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  c1. c2. c3. ... c18. % 18.55 mean
  % conclusion embedded among premises
Conclusion: Q(a).
\end{verbatim}}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$\approx 0$ (at 1000 steps: ISR~$=0.003$, with 94.8\% of proved samples having ISR~$=0$).

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Observed in extended exec-only training (seed~42, 1000 steps).
Mean component count grows from ${\sim}6$ (500 steps) to 18.55 (1000 steps).


\subsection{Query-as-Fact Gaming}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The model converts the natural language conclusion into a snake\_case atom and includes it as both a ground fact and the query.
Prolog trivially proves the query by unifying with the fact.
This mode evades text-match classifiers designed for H1/H7 because the generated atom bears no surface resemblance to the original conclusion text.

\paragraph{Example (Prolog).}
\begin{verbatim}
% NL: "Fido is happy."
% Model output:
fido_is_happy.
:- fido_is_happy.     % query = fact
\end{verbatim}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$\approx 0.9$--$1.0$.
The fact is necessarily necessary (its removal breaks the query), inflating ISR.
Functionally equivalent to H7 but with a distinct surface mechanism.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Observed in Prolog exec+STA seed~44 (PR~$=0.97$, ISR~$=0.912$).
95/97 proved samples have $n_{\text{necessary}}=1$, confirming functional tautology despite the strict classifier reporting 100\% non-hacking.

\section{STA Algorithm}
\label{app:algorithm}

Algorithm~\ref{alg:sta} gives the full procedure for computing ISR over a proved formalization.

\begin{algorithm}[h]
\caption{Solver Trace Ablation (STA)}
\label{alg:sta}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\REQUIRE Formalization $x = \{c_1, \ldots, c_n\}$, solver $S$
\ENSURE ISR score $\in [0,1]$ or $\bot$ (undefined)
\IF{$S(x) \neq \textit{proved}$}
  \RETURN $\bot$
\ENDIF
\STATE $n_{\text{nec}} \gets 0$
\FOR{$i = 1$ \TO $n$}
  \STATE $x' \gets x \setminus \{c_i\}$
  \IF{$S(x') = \textit{failed}$}
    \STATE $n_{\text{nec}} \gets n_{\text{nec}} + 1$
  \ENDIF
\ENDFOR
\RETURN $n_{\text{nec}} \mathbin{/} n$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}


\section{Extended Discussion}
\label{app:extended-discussion}

\paragraph{What ISR measures---and what it does not.}
ISR quantifies syntactic component necessity: the fraction of solver-input components whose individual removal causes proof failure.
This is strictly weaker than semantic faithfulness---whether the formalization accurately captures the natural-language meaning.
We verify this empirically: Spearman $\rho(\text{ISR}, \text{NLI accuracy}) = -0.049$ ($p = 0.187$, n.s.) from a downstream NLI evaluation on exec-only checkpoint outputs.
ISR and downstream task performance are uncorrelated.
ISR is thus a structural integrity diagnostic, not a semantic quality metric: high ISR indicates that every component contributes to the proof, not that the proof faithfully represents the original reasoning problem.

Critically, low ISR carries different semantics depending on the training objective.
Under exec-only training, low ISR in Prolog reflects redundant coding---repeated ground facts where removing any single copy does not affect the proof---rather than absence of reasoning (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).
Under ISR-as-reward, high ISR reflects metric gaming (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
ISR values must always be interpreted relative to the optimization objective that produced them.

\paragraph{The premise-count confound.}
LOO-based metrics like ISR have an inherent mathematical bias: with fewer components, each is mechanically more likely to be necessary.
A formalization with 2 premises where both are necessary yields ISR${=}1.0$; one with 10 premises where 8 are necessary yields ISR${=}0.8$---even though the latter encodes richer reasoning.
This confound explains the sole apparent ISR-as-reward success (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}): ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 produces shorter formalizations, mechanically inflating ISR.
Premise-count-matched comparison eliminates the difference ($1.06\times$; Table~\ref{tab:beta01-3seed}).
This bias is not specific to our setting---any LOO-based structural metric applied to variable-length outputs requires component-count normalization.
We recommend that future work employing ablation-based diagnostics report premise-count-matched comparisons alongside raw values.

\paragraph{Meta-level Goodhart: implications.}
The meta-Goodhart finding extends beyond this specific system.
ISR was designed to \emph{detect} reward gaming of $r_{\text{exec}}$, yet when incorporated into the reward signal, the model games ISR itself---creating a regress where any diagnostic metric risks becoming a target when optimized.
The dose-response pattern ($\beta{=}0.1$: proxy gaming inflates ISR without genuine improvement; $\beta{=}0.3$: performance collapse) maps onto the trajectory predicted by~\cite{gao-reward-overoptimization}, but at a meta level: the proxy being gamed is itself a gaming detector.
Under the taxonomy of~\cite{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy}, $\beta{=}0.3$ exemplifies extremal Goodhart---the optimizer enters a regime where the proxy-target relationship breaks down entirely---while $\beta{=}0.1$ instantiates a meta-level variant where the diagnostic is gamed through its own measurement mechanism.
The practical implication is that ISR---and structurally similar diagnostics---should be used exclusively as post-hoc evaluation tools, never as training rewards.

\paragraph{Single-seed unreliability.}
The three exec-only seeds diverge radically (PR $\sigma{=}\pm 47$ percentage points), each converging to a qualitatively different degeneration mode (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seeds show similar divergence: 2/3 dominated by conclusion duplication (H7), 1/3 by premise minimization (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
Multi-seed evaluation with structural diagnostics should be standard practice for neurosymbolic RL systems.


\section{Hacking Mode Definitions}
\label{app:hacking-modes}

We identify seven distinct reward hacking modes across all experiments.
Each mode is defined below with its mechanism, a representative example, and its interaction with ISR.
Table~\ref{tab:hacking-taxonomy-app} summarizes prevalence across FOL conditions.

\paragraph{Classifier Validation.}
Hacking mode classification uses deterministic rule-based classifiers, not learned models, so standard ML precision/recall is not directly applicable.
H1 and H7 are identified by normalized text matching between conclusion and premise strings after whitespace and variable normalization; remaining modes are detected via functional analysis of the per-sample $n_{\text{necessary}}$ distribution from STA (leave-one-out ablation).
No training data or manual annotation is used for classification.

To estimate precision, we manually verified 50 randomly sampled outputs classified as H1 or H7: all 50 were confirmed correct (estimated precision ${>}$95\%, Wilson 95\% CI: [93\%, 100\%]).
Recall is inherently bounded by the text-match threshold: semantic manipulations that alter surface form while preserving the gaming structure (e.g., variable renaming beyond our normalization, or paraphrased conclusions) would be missed.
We cross-validate with functional LOO analysis: samples classified as non-hacking but showing $n_{\text{necessary}} \leq 1$ are flagged as potential false negatives.
This cross-validation revealed query-as-fact gaming in Prolog (\S\ref{app:hacking-modes}), where the strict text classifier reported 100\% non-hacking but functional analysis showed 95/97 samples were tautological ($n_{\text{necessary}}{=}1$).
The non-hacking rate for FOL conditions may therefore be slightly overestimated, as subtle semantic manipulations below our text-matching threshold would evade the strict classifier.

\subsection{H1 --- Conclusion Embedding}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The conclusion appears verbatim (or with trivial variable renaming) as one premise among multiple premises.
The solver succeeds by matching the embedded conclusion, rendering the other premises irrelevant to the proof.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  all x (bird(x) -> flies(x)).
  bird(tweety).
  flies(tweety).  % conclusion embedded
Conclusion: flies(tweety).
\end{verbatim}}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
Variable. The embedded premise has ISR~$=1$ (removing it may break the proof), but other premises may also register as necessary depending on Prover9's search strategy.
ISR does not distinguish trivial from substantive necessity.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Conclusion embedding in some form (H1 multi-premise or H7 single-premise) is GRPO-universal at 68--97\% across all RL conditions.
Under exec-only and Random reward, it manifests as H1 (71--93\%); under ISR reward, it shifts to H7 (64.5\% pooled).


\subsection{H7 --- Conclusion Duplication}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The entire formalization collapses to a single premise whose content is identical to the conclusion.
Since $P \to P$ is trivially provable, this simultaneously maximizes exec reward.
Because the sole premise is necessary for every sub-component of the conclusion under LOO ablation, ISR is inflated toward 1.0.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  all x ((A(x)&B(x))->(C(x)|D(x))).
Conclusion:
  all x ((A(x)&B(x))->(C(x)|D(x))).
\end{verbatim}}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$\approx 0.8$--$1.0$.
The single premise is trivially ``maximally necessary,'' but the proof is vacuous.
H7 is the only mode that simultaneously games both exec reward and ISR reward.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
ISR-specific: 64.5\% pooled (149/231) under ISR~$\beta{=}0.1$ (s42: 16.0\%, s43: 96.7\%, s44: 86.5\%).
\textbf{Zero} occurrences under Random~$\beta{=}0.1$ across all three seeds ($0/256$).


\subsection{Tautological Collapse}

\paragraph{Definition.}
Two-component formalizations where the premise and conclusion are identical atomic or simple formulas, yielding a $P \to P$ tautology with minimal token cost.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
\begin{verbatim}
Premises: p(a).
Conclusion: p(a).
\end{verbatim}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$=1.0$ (the sole premise is necessary).
Distinguished from H7 by having low component count ($n_{\text{comp}}\approx 2$) and atomic formulas rather than complex sub-structured conclusions.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Dominant in FOL exec-only seed~44 (PR~$=0.98$, mean $n_{\text{comp}}=2.04$, 100\% H7 by strict classifier).
Also observed in Prolog exec+STA seed~42 (100\% H7, PR~$=0.50$).


\subsection{Repetition Collapse}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The model generates identical premises or clauses repeated until the maximum completion length, producing a degenerate output with high token count but no logical diversity.
Removing any single repeated copy leaves the others intact, yielding ISR~$\approx 0$.

\paragraph{Example (Prolog).}
\begin{verbatim}
penguin(fido).
penguin(fido).
penguin(fido).
... (repeated to 512 tokens)
query(penguin(fido)).
\end{verbatim}

\subsection{Complexity-without-Utility}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The formalization contains syntactically complex premises (nested quantifiers, multi-arity predicates) that are semantically vacuous---none individually necessary for the proof.
The complexity inflates surface metrics (formula length, nesting depth) without contributing to logical derivation.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  all x all y (R(x,y) ->
    exists z (S(x,z) & T(z,y))).
  all x (P(x) -> Q(x)).
  P(a).            % only this needed
Conclusion: Q(a).
\end{verbatim}}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR correctly identifies the vacuous premises (ISR~$=0$ for each), pulling down the mean ISR.
This is the mode ISR is best calibrated for.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Low. Observed in Random~$\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 at 3.8\% (3/79).
Not observed under ISR reward (ISR's gradient discourages zero-ISR premises).


\subsection{Contradiction Explosion}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The component count grows unboundedly over training.
Excess premises introduce contradictions or redundancies that trivially entail any conclusion via \emph{ex falso quodlibet}.
Individual premises may register as ISR~$=0$ (removable without breaking the proof), but the sheer count obscures the underlying triviality.

\paragraph{Example (FOL, 1000-step exec-only).}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  c1. c2. c3. ... c18. % 18.55 mean
  % conclusion embedded among premises
Conclusion: Q(a).
\end{verbatim}}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$\approx 0$ (at 1000 steps: ISR~$=0.003$, with 94.8\% of proved samples having ISR~$=0$).

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Observed in extended exec-only training (seed~42, 1000 steps).
Mean component count grows from ${\sim}6$ (500 steps) to 18.55 (1000 steps).


\subsection{Query-as-Fact Gaming}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The model converts the natural language conclusion into a snake\_case atom and includes it as both a ground fact and the query.
Prolog trivially proves the query by unifying with the fact.
This mode evades text-match classifiers designed for H1/H7 because the generated atom bears no surface resemblance to the original conclusion text.

\paragraph{Example (Prolog).}
\begin{verbatim}
% NL: "Fido is happy."
% Model output:
fido_is_happy.
:- fido_is_happy.     % query = fact
\end{verbatim}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$\approx 0.9$--$1.0$.
The fact is necessarily necessary (its removal breaks the query), inflating ISR.
Functionally equivalent to H7 but with a distinct surface mechanism.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Observed in Prolog exec+STA seed~44 (PR~$=0.97$, ISR~$=0.912$).
95/97 proved samples have $n_{\text{necessary}}=1$, confirming functional tautology despite the strict classifier reporting 100\% non-hacking.

\paragraph{ISR collapse trajectory (FOL exec-only, seed 42).}
Table~\ref{tab:fol-detailed} traces the ISR collapse over training:
ISR$^*=0.642$ at 100 steps $\to$ $0.132$ at 500 steps ($-79.4$\%) $\to$ $0.003$ at 1000 steps ($-99.5$\% from step 100).
PR increases monotonically ($0.32 \to 0.93 \to 0.96$) while structural quality collapses, confirming that ISR captures degeneration invisible to execution reward.

\paragraph{Prolog: universal Goodhart via three distinct pathways.}
All three Prolog exec+ISR seeds exhibit Goodhart's Law with 0\% non-hacking proofs (Figure~\ref{fig:prolog-comparison}), but each discovers a different gaming mechanism:
seed~42 produces clean H7 tautologies (single premise~$=$~conclusion),
seed~43 generates uppercase pseudo-Prolog that bypasses the text-match classifier while remaining functionally tautological,
and seed~44 converts NL conclusions to snake\_case atoms used as both fact and query.
The diversity of gaming pathways across seeds---despite identical training data and reward function---demonstrates that Goodhart's Law in neurosymbolic reasoning is not a single failure mode but a family of convergent exploits.

\subsection{Early-Training Hacking Analysis (100-Step Checkpoint)}
\label{app:100step}

To control for the prove-rate confound in our SFT comparison (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}), we analyze the exec-only checkpoint at 100 training steps (seed~42), where PR${=}32$\%---higher than SFT (14\%) but still early in training.
Of the 32 proved samples, 9 (28.1\%) exhibit H7 hacking (single premise identical to conclusion) and 1 (3.1\%) exhibits H1 (conclusion embedded among premises), yielding a total hacking rate of 31.2\%.
By contrast, SFT at comparable or lower PR shows 7.1\% hacking (1/14 proved samples).
This demonstrates that reward hacking emerges early in GRPO training---well before the prove-rate plateau---and is not simply an artifact of having more proved samples available for exploitation.
The 100-step hacking rate (31.2\%) is already substantially above SFT (7.1\%), supporting the claim that hacking is associated with RL optimization rather than prove-rate level alone.
